newsitem.title: CANADA: WIC cuts jobs, posts charge to deepen Q2 loss.
newsitem.headline: WIC cuts jobs, posts charge to deepen Q2 loss.

text.p: Broadcaster WIC Western International Communications Ltd said Friday it had posted a C$8.25 million restructuring charge and 95 layoffs, deepening second quarter losses ahead of fresh competition this year.

Second quarter losses for the three-month period ended February 28 widened to C$3.95 million on revenue of C$113.18 million compared to year earlier C$2.16 million on revenue of C$104.97 million. WIC did not provide per share results.

WIC also took a widely expected C$8.25 million restructuring charge for 95 layoffs on top of earlier job cuts, positioning itself to face stiffer television broadcasting competition in its chief markets of Alberta and British Columbia. It took a C$1.7 million restructuring charge in its year-earlier second quarter.
"WIC TV has been going through a review of its operations in order to position its operations in the environment of the anticipated 100-plus channel universe," it said in a statement.
The new layoffs, which will be phased in over several months, total 51 in Vancouver and 44 in the province of Alberta.

Earlier this year, two rivals were granted licenses for new TV stations in WIC's territory. Craig Broadcast Systems Inc of Manitoba won a license for Alberta while Baton Broadcasting Inc was awarded rights to a new station in Vancouver's highly prized expanding market.

WIC also released its six-month results, posting a profit of C$0.17 a share for the period ended February 28 compared to year-earlier C$0.23 a share. Net earnings totalled C$4.34 million on revenue of C$242.75 million versus year ago profit of C$5.78 million on revenue of C$228.20 million.
A year earlier WIC lost C$2.1 million in its second quarter after expenses of C$2.5 million to cover about 60 layoffs at two television stations.

WIC is under pressure to protect its stations in these two markets since television accounts for about two-thirds of WIC's revenues. It owns eight television stations and a share in Canada's CTV television network among other interests.

The new competition comes on top of a period of turmoil for WIC. Over the past year, it has faced an aborted takeover bid from CanWest Global Communications Corp, dissatisfied shareholders who critized its performance, a shufffle in top management and a failed lawsuit after the founding Griffiths family refused to hand over company control.
